did_you_know.text: Did you know? The vision opens with four chariots emerging from between two mountains, and the mountains are described as “mountains of bronze”—a description emphasizing their powerful and extraordinary appearance.

Did you know? Each chariot has horses of different colors: red, black, white, and dappled. The colors are a central part of the vision’s description, but the chapter does not explicitly explain the meaning of each color.
Did you know? The angel explains that the four chariots represent “the four spirits of heaven,” going out after presenting themselves before the Lord of all the earth.
Did you know? The chariot with the black horses goes toward the land of the north, the white horses follow them, and the dappled horses go toward the land of the south.
Did you know? The strong horses ask to patrol the earth, and the angel allows them to go. They then do indeed patrol the earth as part of the movement of the chariots in the vision.

Did you know? Regarding the chariots going to the land of the north, it is said that they bring the Lord’s spirit to rest in the land of the north. This describes a special result of their mission in the vision.

Did you know? Zechariah is commanded to take silver and gold from the exiles—Heldai, Tobijah, and Jedaiah—who have arrived from Babylon, and to go that same day to the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah.

Did you know? He is commanded to make a crown from the silver and gold and place it on the head of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. In this way, the vision connects the contribution of those returning from Babylon with the leadership of the people and the rebuilding of the Temple.

Did you know? The chapter introduces a figure called “the Branch,” of whom it is said that he will sprout from his place and build the Temple of the Lord. In context, he is presented as having a central role in the Temple’s renewal; the chapter itself does not mention Zerubbabel by name here.

Did you know? The prophecy describes a combination of governing authority and priesthood: “the Branch” will bear majesty and sit on his throne, with a priest beside him, and there will be “a peaceful council” between the two of them.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, it says that people from far away will come and build the Temple of the Lord. However, the fulfillment of these words is presented as depending also on listening to the voice of the Lord, not merely on the act of building itself.
